title: Ἄρεος καὶ Ἴριδος ἀγγελίαι
titleEn: Ares Held Back, Iris Sent — Iliad 15.92–183
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Hera, back among the gods, will not tell Themis what Zeus is like and bitterly warns the banquet to expect trouble. She stirs up the table, and Ares, hearing that his son Ascalaphus is dead, strikes his thighs and calls for his horses to go and avenge him in defiance of Zeus. Athena, afraid of the consequences, disarms him and talks him down. Hera then sends Apollo and Iris to Zeus on Ida, who is not angry. Zeus sends Iris to tell Poseidon to leave the fight, and Iris carries the message down to the plain, repeating Zeus's boast of his greater strength and age.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita thea leukōlenos Hērē·
sentences.l: Her then answered the goddess, white-armed Hera:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, white-armed Hera, answered her:
sentences.n: This is the whole-line reply formula, with the same verb as ‘Him then answered’ elsewhere; Hera is answering Themis, whose question ended the last part. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’; τήν ‘her’ is the old pronoun-article. θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη is a stock epithet, ‘white-armed’, translated every time.

sentences.t: μή με θεὰ Θέμι ταῦτα διείρεο·
sentences.tr: mē me thea Themi tauta dieireo·
sentences.l: “Not me, goddess Themis, these things question;
sentences.i: “Do not question me about these things, goddess Themis;
sentences.n: Hera is refusing to explain herself to Themis. θεὰ Θέμι is a vocative, ‘goddess Themis’, the goddess who welcomed her with the cup at the end of the last part. μή with the imperative διείρεο (present of διείρομαι, ‘ask through, question closely’) is a prohibition: ‘do not keep questioning me’.

sentences.t:
οἶσθα καὶ αὐτὴ
οἷος κείνου θυμὸς ὑπερφίαλος καὶ ἀπηνής.
sentences.tr:
oistha kai autē
hoios keinou thymos hyperphialos kai apēnēs.
sentences.l:
you know, even yourself,
what sort of heart that one’s is, overweening and unkind.
sentences.i: you know it yourself: what sort of heart his is, overweening and unkind.
sentences.n: οἶσθα ‘you know’ is the perfect-as-present of οἶδα. κείνου ‘of that one’ is the Ionic-epic form of ἐκείνου, and the person meant, Zeus, is not named. Both adjectives are the house words: ὑπερφίαλος ‘overweening’, ἀπηνής ‘unkind’; the Greek gives no further hint of their origin, and ἀπηνής is of uncertain derivation.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σύ γ’ ἄρχε θεοῖσι δόμοις ἔνι δαιτὸς ἐΐσης·
sentences.tr: alla sy g’ arche theoisi domois eni daitos eïsēs·
sentences.l: But you at least begin, for the gods, in the halls, the equal feast;
sentences.i: But you, for your part, begin the equally shared feast for the gods in the halls;
sentences.n: Hera tells Themis to carry on with the banquet. ἄρχε is the present imperative of ἄρχω, ‘begin, lead’, with the genitive of the thing begun, δαιτός ‘of the feast’. δαιτὸς ἐΐσης is the old formula ‘the equal feast’, where every guest has his share. δόμοις ἔνι is ‘in the halls’, with ἔνι = ἐν after its noun; θεοῖσι is the dative ‘for the gods’.

sentences.t:
ταῦτα δὲ καὶ μετὰ πᾶσιν ἀκούσεαι ἀθανάτοισιν
οἷα Ζεὺς κακὰ ἔργα πιφαύσκεται·
sentences.tr:
tauta de kai meta pasin akouseai athanatoisin
hoia Zeus kaka erga piphausketai·
sentences.l:
And these things also, among all the immortals, you will hear,
what sort of evil deeds Zeus is making known;
sentences.i: and you will hear these things too, among all the immortals: what sort of evil deeds Zeus is making known;
sentences.n: ἀκούσεαι is the future of ἀκούω, ‘you will hear’, with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ). μετὰ πᾶσιν … ἀθανάτοισιν is ‘among all the immortals’, i.e. when the gods are gathered. οἷα … ἔργα is an indirect exclamation, ‘what sort of deeds’; πιφαύσκεται is the middle of πιφαύσκω ‘make known, show forth’, here ‘announces by his actions’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί φημι
πᾶσιν ὁμῶς θυμὸν κεχαρησέμεν, οὔτε βροτοῖσιν
οὔτε θεοῖς, εἴ πέρ τις ἔτι νῦν δαίνυται εὔφρων.
sentences.tr:
oude ti phēmi
pasin homōs thymon kecharēsemen, oute brotoisin
oute theois, ei per tis eti nyn dainytai euphrōn.
sentences.l:
and not at all, I say,
in heart will all alike be glad, neither mortals
nor gods, if indeed anyone still now feasts, cheerful.”
sentences.i: and I say that not all alike will be glad at heart, neither mortals nor gods, even if someone is still feasting cheerfully now.”
sentences.n: The sentence is a bitter forecast: οὐδέ τί φημι ‘and I say not at all’ turns the negative on the infinitive, so ‘I say that they will not be glad’. κεχαρησέμεν is the reduplicated future infinitive of χαίρω, ‘will be glad’; θυμόν is the accusative of respect, ‘in heart’. εἴ πέρ τις ἔτι νῦν δαίνυται εὔφρων concedes that someone may be feasting happily now. The speech ends with the line.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσα καθέζετο πότνια Ἥρη,
ὄχθησαν δ’ ἀνὰ δῶμα Διὸς θεοί·
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs eipousa kathezeto potnia Hērē,
ochthēsan d’ ana dōma Dios theoi·
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken sat down, lady Hera,
and were vexed, throughout the house of Zeus, the gods;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and lady Hera sat down, and throughout the house of Zeus the gods were troubled;
sentences.n: The speech is over and the room reacts. ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσα … is a whole-line formula for ‘so she spoke, and…’, with ἣ μέν ‘she on her part’ balanced by ἣ δ’ in the next clause. πότνια Ἥρη is ‘lady Hera’. ὄχθησαν is an aorist of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed’; the verb comes before its subject θεοί, which is held to the end of the line.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐγέλασσε
χείλεσιν, οὐδὲ μέτωπον ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι κυανέῃσιν
ἰάνθη·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ egelasse
cheilesin, oude metōpon ep’ ophrysi kyaneēisin
ianthē·
sentences.i: and she laughed with her lips alone, and her forehead above her dark brows was not cheered;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is Hera again. She laughs, but only χείλεσιν ‘with her lips’ (a dative of means). ἰάνθη is the aorist passive of ἰαίνω, ‘warm’, and in the mind ‘cheer’: the laugh does not reach her brow. κυανέῃσιν, ‘dark’ (the word for a deep blue-black), has the epic dative ending -ῃσιν, and οὐδὲ … ἰάνθη ‘was not … warmed’ carries over the line-end.

sentences.t: πᾶσιν δὲ νεμεσσηθεῖσα μετηύδα·
sentences.tr: pasin de nemessētheisa metēuda·
sentences.l: and at them all, feeling resentment, she spoke among them:
sentences.i: and, resentful at them all, she spoke among them:
sentences.n: νεμεσσηθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of νεμεσσάω, the Odyssey’s ‘feel resentment’, a righteous indignation at others’ conduct; here it is aimed at the whole company, πᾶσιν. μετηύδα is the imperfect ‘spoke among them’ (μετά ‘among’ + ηὔδα), the usual verb for an address to an assembly.

sentences.t: νήπιοι οἳ Ζηνὶ μενεαίνομεν ἀφρονέοντες·
sentences.tr: nēpioi hoi Zēni meneainomen aphroneontes·
sentences.l: “Foolish ones, we who against Zeus rage, being witless;
sentences.i: “How foolish we are, raging against Zeus in our witlessness;
sentences.n: Hera now includes herself with the other gods (μενεαίνομεν ‘we rage’). νήπιοι ‘foolish’ is a nominative of exclamation (‘fools that we are’), a stock word for blind folly; ἀφρονέοντες is the uncontracted participle of ἀφρονέω ‘be witless, not think’ (Attic ἀφρονοῦντες). Ζηνί is the dative of Ζεύς, with its stem Ζην-.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἔτι μιν μέμαμεν καταπαυσέμεν ἆσσον ἰόντες
ἢ ἔπει ἠὲ βίῃ·
sentences.tr:
ē eti min memamen katapausemen asson iontes
ē epei ēe biēi·
sentences.l:
Truly still we are eager to check him, going close up,
either by word or by force;
sentences.i: We are still eager, truly, to check him by going close up to him, whether with a word or by force;
sentences.n: ἦ ἔτι is ‘truly, even now’. μέμαμεν is the perfect (as present) of a verb meaning ‘be eager’, with the infinitive καταπαυσέμεν (epic -έμεν for -εῖν) ‘to stop, bring to a halt’. ἔπει is the dative of ἔπος, ‘by a word’, matched with ἠὲ βίῃ ‘or by force’; the contrast of word and force is what Hera has in mind.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀφήμενος οὐκ ἀλεγίζει
οὐδ’ ὄθεται·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ aphēmenos ouk alegizei
oud’ othetai·
sentences.l:
but he, sitting aloof, does not care
and takes no heed;
sentences.i: but he sits aloof and does not care, and takes no heed;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Zeus, contrasted with the gods who rage. ἀφήμενος is the participle of ἀφῆμαι ‘sit apart, aloof’. ἀλεγίζει ‘cares for’ and ὄθεται ‘heeds’ are near neighbours; both are negated, and the unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 107.

sentences.t:
φησὶν γὰρ ἐν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι
κάρτεΐ τε σθένεΐ τε διακριδὸν εἶναι ἄριστος.
sentences.tr:
phēsin gar en athanatoisi theoisi
karteï te stheneï te diakridon einai aristos.
sentences.l:
for he says that among the immortal gods
in strength and in power, distinctly, he is best.
sentences.i: for he says that among the immortal gods he is distinctly the best, in strength and in power.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for Zeus’s indifference: his boast. φησίν is ‘he says’, with the infinitive εἶναι. κάρτεΐ τε σθένεΐ τε are datives of respect from κάρτος and σθένος, two words for strength and power; the diaeresis shows that the final syllable is to be sounded separately. διακριδόν is ‘distinctly, by a clear margin’.

sentences.t: τὼ ἔχεθ’ ὅττί κεν ὔμμι κακὸν πέμπῃσιν ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.tr: tō echeth’ hotti ken ymmi kakon pempēisin hekastōi.
sentences.l: Therefore bear whatever evil he may send to each of you.
sentences.i: So bear whatever evil he may send to each of you.
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore, so’. ἔχεθ’ is ἔχετε with its last vowel dropped and the τ made rough before the rough breathing of ὅττι, so it is the imperative ‘hold, put up with’. ὅττι κεν … πέμπῃσιν is an indefinite clause, κεν (= ἄν) with the subjunctive ‘whatever he may send’; ὔμμι is the epic ‘to you’ (plural).

sentences.t: ἤδη γὰρ νῦν ἔλπομ’ Ἄρηΐ γε πῆμα τετύχθαι·
sentences.tr: ēdē gar nyn elpom’ Arēï ge pēma tetychthai·
sentences.l: For already now I expect that for Ares at least a woe has been made;
sentences.i: For I expect that by now a woe has been made for Ares, at least;
sentences.n: ἔλπομ’ is ἔλπομαι, which means ‘expect’ (including bad things), not ‘hope’. γε limits the claim to Ares: he, at least, has already been struck. τετύχθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of τεύχω ‘make’: ‘a woe has been made (for him)’, and πῆμα is ‘woe’. Ἄρηΐ is the dative of the god Ares with its diaeresis.

sentences.t:
υἱὸς γάρ οἱ ὄλωλε μάχῃ ἔνι φίλτατος ἀνδρῶν
Ἀσκάλαφος, τόν φησιν ὃν ἔμμεναι ὄβριμος Ἄρης.
sentences.tr:
huios gar hoi olōle machēi eni philtatos andrōn
Askalaphos, ton phēsin hon emmenai obrimos Arēs.
sentences.l:
for his son has perished in the fight, dearest of men,
Ascalaphus, whom he says is his own, mighty Ares.”
sentences.i: for his son has died in battle, the dearest of men to him, Ascalaphus, whom mighty Ares says is his own.”
sentences.n: Hera explains the woe: Ascalaphus, a son of Ares, has been killed in the fighting. ὄλωλε is the perfect of ὄλλυμι ‘be lost, perish’; οἱ ‘to him’ is the dative of interest. In τόν φησιν ὃν ἔμμεναι the second ὅν is the possessive, ‘his own’, not the relative; ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. The speech ends here. Ἄρης is the god, and ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ is his stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ Ἄρης θαλερὼ πεπλήγετο μηρὼ
χερσὶ καταπρηνέσσ’, ὀλοφυρόμενος δ’ ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar Arēs thalerō peplēgeto mērō
chersi kataprēness’, olophyromenos d’ epos ēuda·
sentences.l:
So she spoke, but Ares his two flourishing thighs struck
with downturned hands, and lamenting a word he spoke:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and Ares struck both his flourishing thighs with the flats of his hands, and as he lamented he spoke:
sentences.n: Ares takes in the news and responds with the gesture of grief: the struck thighs, as in the Odyssey, from which the second line is taken whole. θαλερὼ … μηρὼ are duals, ‘the two thighs’; θαλερός is ‘flourishing’ (full of life). καταπρηνέσσ’ is ‘downturned’, hands with palms flat. ἔπος ηὔδα is the formula for ‘he spoke’.

sentences.t:
μὴ νῦν μοι νεμεσήσετ’ Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
τίσασθαι φόνον υἷος ἰόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν,
εἴ πέρ μοι καὶ μοῖρα Διὸς πληγέντι κεραυνῷ
κεῖσθαι ὁμοῦ νεκύεσσι μεθ’ αἵματι καὶ κονίῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
mē nyn moi nemesēset’ Olympia dōmat’ echontes
tisasthai phonon huios iont’ epi nēas Achaiōn,
ei per moi kai moira Dios plēgenti keraunōi
keisthai homou nekyessi meth’ haimati kai koniēisin.
sentences.l:
“Do not now feel resentment at me, you who hold the Olympian halls,
to avenge the killing of my son, going to the ships of the Achaeans,
even if it is my portion too, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus,
to lie together with the corpses in blood and in dust.”
sentences.i: “Do not now feel resentment at me, you who hold the halls of Olympus, for going to the ships of the Achaeans to avenge my son’s killing; even if it is my portion too to be struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus and to lie with the corpses in blood and in dust.”
sentences.n: Ares addresses the gods collectively: Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες ‘who hold the Olympian halls’ is the usual way to say ‘gods’. μὴ νεμεσήσετ’ is a prohibition, the aorist subjunctive (with a short vowel) of νεμεσσάω, ‘do not feel resentment’. τίσασθαι φόνον is ‘to exact payment for the killing’, a phrase of vengeance, and ἰόντ’ ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν is ‘going to the ships of the Achaeans’ (ἰόντ’ the accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed ‘me’). εἴ πέρ … ‘even if’ opens a fate he is ready to meet: Zeus’s thunderbolt. Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’ is one of the army’s three names.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καί ῥ’ ἵππους κέλετο Δεῖμόν τε Φόβον τε
ζευγνύμεν, αὐτὸς δ’ ἔντε’ ἐδύσετο παμφανόωντα.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, kai rh’ hippous keleto Deimon te Phobon te
zeugnymen, autos d’ ente’ edyseto pamphanoōnta.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and then he bade Dread and Terror the horses
to yoke, while himself he put on the gear, all-shining.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and bade Dread and Terror yoke the horses, and he himself put on his all-shining gear.
sentences.n: Δεῖμον and Φόβον, ‘Dread’ and ‘Terror’, are the personified powers that go to battle with Ares (as at 4.440); here they act as his grooms, and are the accusative subject of ζευγνύμεν ‘to yoke’, with ἵππους its object. κέλετο is the unaugmented ‘bade’. ἔντε’ is ἔντεα ‘gear’, with ἐδύσετο ‘put on’ (middle of δύω); παμφανόωντα ‘all-shining’ is the uncontracted accusative plural. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of κέλετο, short by nature, has to stand in the long place of the fourth foot, as if Δεῖμον still began with a double consonant (the old digamma).

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κ’ ἔτι μείζων τε καὶ ἀργαλεώτερος ἄλλος
πὰρ Διὸς ἀθανάτοισι χόλος καὶ μῆνις ἐτύχθη,
sentences.tr:
entha k’ eti meizōn te kai argaleōteros allos
par Dios athanatoisi cholos kai mēnis etychthē,
sentences.l:
Then would a still greater and more grievous other
from Zeus, among the immortals, anger and wrath have been made,
sentences.i: Then a still greater and more grievous anger and wrath would have been stirred up among the immortals, from Zeus,
sentences.n: ἔνθά κ’ ‘then … would’ begins an unreal condition: this is what would have happened, but for Athena (123). μείζων and ἀργαλεώτερος are comparatives, ‘greater’ and ‘more grievous’, belonging to χόλος ‘anger’ and μῆνις ‘wrath’; ἄλλος ‘another, further’ adds ‘still more’. πὰρ Διός is ‘from Zeus’s side’. ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω ‘was made, came about’, and the sentence runs on to the condition in the next unit.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὴ Ἀθήνη πᾶσι περιδείσασα θεοῖσιν
ὦρτο διὲκ προθύρου, λίπε δὲ θρόνον ἔνθα θάασσε,
sentences.tr:
ei mē Athēnē pasi perideisasa theoisin
ōrto diek prothyrou, lipe de thronon entha thaasse,
sentences.l:
had not Athena, fearing greatly for all the gods,
rushed through the forecourt, and left the seat where she was sitting,
sentences.i: if Athena, in great fear for all the gods, had not sprung up and rushed out through the forecourt, leaving the seat where she was sitting,
sentences.n: εἰ μή ‘if not’ is the other half of the unreal condition. περιδείσασα is the aorist participle of περιδείδω ‘fear greatly (for)’, with πᾶσι … θεοῖσιν ‘for all the gods’ in the dative. ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘rose, sprang’, with διὲκ προθύρου ‘out through the forecourt’ (the court before the entrance of the hall); θάασσε is the imperfect ‘was sitting’. Ἀθήνη is the epic-Ionic form of Attic Ἀθηνᾶ.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν κεφαλῆς κόρυθ’ εἵλετο καὶ σάκος ὤμων,
ἔγχος δ’ ἔστησε στιβαρῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα
χάλκεον·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ apo men kephalēs koryth’ heileto kai sakos ōmōn,
enchos d’ estēse stibarēs apo cheiros helousa
chalkeon·
sentences.i: she took the helmet from his head and the shield from his shoulders, and took the bronze spear from his stout hand and stood it upright;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘from him’ is Ares, whom she disarms before he can ride out. ἀπὸ … εἵλετο is tmesis, the preverb ἀπό ‘away’ standing apart from εἵλετο ‘took’. ἔστησε is ‘made stand, set upright’. στιβαρῆς is ‘stout’, said of the hand, ἑλοῦσα is the participle ‘having taken it’, and χάλκεον ‘bronze’, the spear’s epithet, is held over to the start of line 127.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἐπέεσσι καθάπτετο θοῦρον Ἄρηα·
sentences.tr: hē d’ epeessi kathapteto thouron Arēa·
sentences.l: and she with words accosted impetuous Ares:
sentences.i: and she addressed impetuous Ares directly in words:
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is Athena. ἐπέεσσι καθάπτετο is ‘accosted with words’, καθάπτομαι meaning ‘lay hold of, address’ and so a sharp, direct address. θοῦρον is the house epithet ‘impetuous’; Ἄρηα is the accusative of Ἄρης, with its epic ending -α.

sentences.t: μαινόμενε φρένας ἠλὲ διέφθορας·
sentences.tr: mainomene phrenas ēle diephthoras·
sentences.l: “Raging one, distraught in your wits, you are ruined;
sentences.i: “You are raging, distraught one; your wits are ruined;
sentences.n: Athena opens with two vocatives, μαινόμενε ‘raging one’ and ἠλέ ‘distraught one’ (ἠλός, ‘crazed, out of one’s senses’). φρένας is the accusative of respect, ‘in your wits’, and διέφθορας is the perfect of διαφθείρω ‘destroy’, in its intransitive sense: ‘you are destroyed, undone’.

sentences.t:
ἦ νύ τοι αὔτως
οὔατ’ ἀκουέμεν ἐστί, νόος δ’ ἀπόλωλε καὶ αἰδώς.
sentences.tr:
ē ny toi autōs
ouat’ akouemen esti, noos d’ apolōle kai aidōs.
sentences.l:
Truly, for you, just so, ears
for hearing there are, and your mind is lost, and shame.
sentences.i: Truly, you have ears for hearing for nothing, and your mind has perished, and your sense of shame.
sentences.n: ἦ νύ τοι is ‘truly, then, for you’. αὔτως is ‘just so, to no purpose’: the ears are there and do nothing. οὔατ’ is the epic οὔατα ‘ears’, the elided plural, with ἀκουέμεν the epic infinitive of ἀκούω. ἀπόλωλε is the perfect of ἀπόλλυμι ‘has perished’, and αἰδώς is ‘shame’, the feeling that restrains one from acting disgracefully.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἀΐεις ἅ τέ φησι θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
ἣ δὴ νῦν πὰρ Ζηνὸς Ὀλυμπίου εἰλήλουθεν;
sentences.tr:
ouk aïeis ha te phēsi thea leukōlenos Hērē
hē dē nyn par Zēnos Olympiou eilēlouthen;
sentences.l:
Do you not hear what she says, the goddess, white-armed Hera,
who now has come from Olympian Zeus?
sentences.i: Do you not hear what the goddess, white-armed Hera, says, she who has just now come from Olympian Zeus?
sentences.n: ἀΐεις is the present of ἀΐω ‘hear, perceive’, with its diaeresis. ἅ τέ φησι is ‘what she says’, with the epic τε, which adds no meaning here. ἣ δή is the relative ‘she who, indeed’, and εἰλήλουθεν is the perfect of ἔρχομαι ‘has come’ (Attic ἐλήλυθεν). The question ends in the Greek question mark. Zeus is Ὀλύμπιος ‘Olympian’ by epithet.

sentences.l:
Or do you wish, having yourself filled up many evils,
to go back to Olympus, grieving though you be, under compulsion,
but for all the others to plant a great evil?
sentences.i: Or do you wish, after filling up the measure of many evils yourself, to go back to Olympus, grieving though you are, under compulsion, and to plant a great evil for all the rest?
sentences.n: ἦ ἐθέλεις asks ‘or do you really wish…?’, with two infinitives resting on ἐθέλεις, ἴμεν (epic for ἰέναι ‘to go’) and φυτεῦσαι ‘to plant’, and the aorist participle ἀναπλήσας ‘having filled up’ the evils, i.e. suffered them to the full. Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’ with the -δε of direction; ἀνάγκῃ is ‘by compulsion’. The ‘planting’ of evil is Homer’s image for causing harm.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα γὰρ Τρῶας μὲν ὑπερθύμους καὶ Ἀχαιοὺς
λείψει, ὃ δ’ ἡμέας εἶσι κυδοιμήσων ἐς Ὄλυμπον,
μάρψει δ’ ἑξείης ὅς τ’ αἴτιος ὅς τε καὶ οὐκί.
sentences.tr:
autika gar Trōas men hyperthymous kai Achaious
leipsei, ho d’ hēmeas eisi kydoimēsōn es Olympon,
marpsei d’ hexeiēs hos t’ aitios hos te kai ouki.
sentences.l:
For at once the Trojans, high-spirited, and the Achaeans
he will leave, and he will come to us, to throw us into uproar, to Olympus,
and will seize in order whoever is guilty and whoever is not.
sentences.i: For at once he will leave the high-spirited Trojans and the Achaeans, and come to Olympus to throw us into uproar, and will seize us in order, whoever is to blame and whoever is not.
sentences.n: Athena says what Zeus will do if Ares goes back to the fight: ὃ δ’ ‘he’ is Zeus, never named. λείψει is the future of λείπω ‘leave’. κυδοιμήσων is a future participle of purpose, ‘to make uproar among’; the rare verb comes from κυδοιμός ‘the din of battle’. μάρψει δ’ ἑξείης is ‘and he will seize in order’; οὐκί is the epic οὐχί, ‘not’. ὑπερθύμους ‘high-spirited’ stands next to Τρῶας and may go with Ἀχαιούς too; the English puts it with the Trojans.

sentences.t: τώ σ’ αὖ νῦν κέλομαι μεθέμεν χόλον υἷος ἑῆος·
sentences.tr: tō s’ au nyn kelomai methemen cholon huios heēos·
sentences.l: Therefore I now bid you, in turn, let go the anger for your own son;
sentences.i: So I now bid you in turn to let go your anger for your own son;
sentences.n: τώ is ‘therefore’ again; αὖ ‘in turn’ and σ’ is σε ‘you’. μεθέμεν is the epic infinitive of μεθίημι ‘let go’, the same verb as ‘let go his anger’ elsewhere; χόλον υἷος is ‘the anger for the sake of the son’. ἑῆος is a form of the possessive ἑός ‘own’, agreeing with υἷος, so ‘your own son’, not the relative (it is sometimes taken instead as the genitive of ἐΰς ‘good’; ‘own’ is followed).

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ τις τοῦ γε βίην καὶ χεῖρας ἀμείνων
ἢ πέφατ’, ἢ καὶ ἔπειτα πεφήσεται·
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar tis tou ge biēn kai cheiras ameinōn
ē pephat’, ē kai epeita pephēsetai·
sentences.l:
For already someone, than he in might and in hands better,
has been slain, or even hereafter will be slain;
sentences.i: For already someone better than he in might and in hand has been slain, or will be slain hereafter;
sentences.n: Athena argues that death takes better men than Ascalaphus. τοῦ γε is ‘than he’ (the genitive of comparison after ἀμείνων ‘better’), and βίην καὶ χεῖρας are accusatives of respect: ‘in might and in hands’. πέφατ’ is the perfect passive of φένω ‘slay’ (πέφαται, with the final vowel gone); πεφήσεται is its future passive, and both are the same verb with different tenses: ‘has been slain’, ‘will be slain’.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δὲ
πάντων ἀνθρώπων ῥῦσθαι γενεήν τε τόκον τε.
sentences.tr:
argaleon de
pantōn anthrōpōn rhysthai geneēn te tokon te.
sentences.l:
and hard it is
of all men to protect the lineage and the birth.”
sentences.i: and it is hard to protect the lineage and the birth of all men.”
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον δέ ‘and hard it is’ gives the general truth behind the case: no one can shield his whole line from death. ῥῦσθαι is the infinitive of ῥύομαι ‘protect, rescue’. γενεήν ‘lineage’ and τόκον ‘birth’ are the two objects, both governed by πάντων ἀνθρώπων ‘of all men’. The speech ends here. This unit begins in the middle of line 140.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἵδρυσε θρόνῳ ἔνι θοῦρον Ἄρηα.
sentences.tr: hōs eipous’ hidryse thronōi eni thouron Arēa.
sentences.l: So having spoken, she seated on the throne impetuous Ares.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and seated impetuous Ares on the throne.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is the formula ‘so having spoken’; ἵδρυσε is the aorist of ἱδρύω ‘cause to sit, seat’, and θρόνῳ ἔνι is ‘on the throne’ (the seat is not named; presumably it is his own), ἔνι standing after its noun. The line shows Ares obeying. θοῦρον is the stock ‘impetuous’.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη δ’ Ἀπόλλωνα καλέσσατο δώματος ἐκτὸς
Ἶρίν θ’, ἥ τε θεοῖσι μετάγγελος ἀθανάτοισι,
καί σφεας φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
Hērē d’ Apollōna kalessato dōmatos ektos
Irin th’, hē te theoisi metangelos athanatoisi,
kai spheas phōnēsas’ epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And Hera Apollo summoned, outside the house,
and Iris, who among the immortal gods is a messenger,
and, lifting her voice, to them winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: Hera called Apollo out of the house, and Iris, who is a messenger among the immortal gods, and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: Hera now carries out Zeus’s instruction from the last part. καλέσσατο is the aorist of καλέω ‘call’, with δώματος ἐκτός ‘outside the house’; Ἶρίν θ’ is ‘and Iris’. ἥ τε is the relative with epic τε; μετάγγελος is a rare word, ‘messenger among’ (μετά ‘among’ + ἄγγελος), explained by the dative θεοῖσι … ἀθανάτοισι. καί σφεας φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the whole-line formula, ‘winged words’, translated every time; σφεας is ‘them’.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς σφὼ εἰς Ἴδην κέλετ’ ἐλθέμεν ὅττι τάχιστα·
sentences.tr: Zeus sphō eis Idēn kelet’ elthemen hotti tachista·
sentences.l: “Zeus bids you two go to Ida as quickly as possible;
sentences.i: “Zeus bids you two go to Ida as quickly as you can;
sentences.n: σφώ is the dual ‘you two’ (Apollo and Iris), and ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι ‘to go’. κέλετ’ is κέλεται, ‘he bids’. ὅττι τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’, the standard idiom with a superlative. Ἴδη is the mountain near Troy where Zeus sits.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν ἔλθητε, Διός τ’ εἰς ὦπα ἴδησθε,
ἕρδειν ὅττί κε κεῖνος ἐποτρύνῃ καὶ ἀνώγῃ.
sentences.tr:
autar epēn elthēte, Dios t’ eis ōpa idēsthe,
herdein hotti ke keinos epotrynēi kai anōgēi.
sentences.l:
but when you two have come, and into the face of Zeus have looked,
do whatever that one may urge on and bid.”
sentences.i: and when you have come and looked Zeus in the face, do whatever he may urge and bid.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν is ‘but when’ (ἐπὴν = ἐπεὶ ἄν); ἔλθητε and ἴδησθε are aorist subjunctives, ‘you have come… have looked’ (the plural ending -τε is used, though only two are addressed). εἰς ὦπα is ‘into the face’. ἕρδειν is an infinitive used as a command, ‘do!’. ὅττί κε … ἐποτρύνῃ καὶ ἀνώγῃ is an indefinite clause, ‘whatever that one may urge and bid’, with κεῖνος ‘that one’, Zeus. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσα πάλιν κίε πότνια Ἥρη,
ἕζετο δ’ εἰνὶ θρόνῳ·
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs eipousa palin kie potnia Hērē,
hezeto d’ eini thronōi·
sentences.l:
She, indeed, then so having spoken went back, lady Hera,
and sat down on the throne;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and lady Hera went back, and sat down on the throne;
sentences.n: The same formula as at 100 begins: ἣ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσα ‘so she spoke, and…’; κίε is the unaugmented imperfect ‘went’, and πάλιν ‘back’. ἕζετο is ‘sat down’, and εἰνί is the poetic form of ἐνί, ‘on’. Hera has done what Zeus asked, and the scene shifts.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἀΐξαντε πετέσθην.
sentences.tr: tō d’ aïxante petesthēn.
sentences.l: and the two, darting off, flew.
sentences.i: and the two of them darted off and flew.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article, ‘the two’ (Apollo and Iris). ἀΐξαντε is a dual aorist participle of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, and πετέσθην a dual of πέτομαι ‘fly’; the dual forms say that the two move as one.

sentences.t:
Ἴδην δ’ ἵκανον πολυπίδακα μητέρα θηρῶν,
εὗρον δ’ εὐρύοπα Κρονίδην ἀνὰ Γαργάρῳ ἄκρῳ
ἥμενον·
sentences.tr:
Idēn d’ hikanon polypidaka mētera thērōn,
heuron d’ euryopa Kronidēn ana Gargarōi akrōi
hēmenon·
sentences.i: They came to Ida of many springs, mother of wild beasts, and found the son of Cronus, who thunders from afar, sitting on the peak of Gargarus;
sentences.n: Ἴδην … πολυπίδακα μητέρα θηρῶν is the stock description of Ida, ‘many-fountained, mother of wild beasts’. ἵκανον is the imperfect of ἱκάνω, without the augment; εὗρον is the aorist ‘found’. εὐρύοπα Κρονίδην is ‘far-thundering the son of Cronus’, Zeus; εὐρύοπα is not certainly understood. Γαργάρῳ ἄκρῳ is the topmost peak of Ida, with ἀνά + dative ‘on’; ἥμενον ‘sitting’ ends the clause with the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δέ μιν θυόεν νέφος ἐστεφάνωτο.
sentences.tr: amphi de min thyoen nephos estephanōto.
sentences.l: and about him a fragrant cloud was set as a crown.
sentences.i: and a fragrant cloud was set like a crown about him.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … ἐστεφάνωτο is a tmesis, the preverb standing apart from the verb; the pluperfect passive of στεφανόω ‘wreathe, crown’ gives the picture of a cloud set round Zeus’s head. θυόεν is ‘fragrant’, as of incense (θύος). μιν is ‘him’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ πάροιθ’ ἐλθόντε Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο
στήτην·
sentences.tr:
tō de paroith’ elthonte Dios nephelēgeretao
stētēn·
sentences.l:
And the two, having come before cloud-gatherer Zeus,
stood;
sentences.i: And the two came and stood before Zeus who gathers the clouds;
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article again, ‘the two’. πάροιθ’ is ‘before, in front of’, with the genitive Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο ‘of cloud-gatherer Zeus’, the stock epithet translated every time. ἐλθόντε is a dual participle, and στήτην the dual of ἔστην ‘stood’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σφωϊν ἰδὼν ἐχολώσατο θυμῷ,
ὅττί οἱ ὦκ’ ἐπέεσσι φίλης ἀλόχοιο πιθέσθην.
sentences.tr:
oude sphōïn idōn echolōsato thymōi,
hotti hoi ōk’ epeessi philēs alochoio pithesthēn.
sentences.l:
and he did not, at the two, seeing them, become angry in his heart,
because quickly to the words of his dear wife they had obeyed.
sentences.i: and he was not angered in his heart at the sight of the two of them, because they had quickly obeyed the words of his dear wife.
sentences.n: σφωϊν is the dual dative ‘at the two’, with ἰδών ‘seeing’. ἐχολώσατο is the aorist of χολόω ‘be angered’. ὅττι is ὅτι ‘because’; οἱ is ‘his’, belonging with φίλης ἀλόχοιο ‘dear wife’. πιθέσθην is the dual aorist middle of πείθω, ‘they obeyed’, which takes the dative ἐπέεσσι ‘to the words’. Zeus had told Hera to send them, and they have come at once.

sentences.t: Ἶριν δὲ προτέρην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: Irin de proterēn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: And to Iris first winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And to Iris first he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: The subject, Zeus, is not named. προτέρην is ‘first’, i.e. before Apollo; Ἶριν is the object of the verb προσηύδα, ‘spoke to’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase, translated every time. The speech follows.

sentences.t:
βάσκ’ ἴθι Ἶρι ταχεῖα, Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι
πάντα τάδ’ ἀγγεῖλαι, μὴ δὲ ψευδάγγελος εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
bask’ ithi Iri tacheia, Poseidaōni anakti
panta tad’ angeilai, mē de pseudangelos einai.
sentences.l:
“Go, set out, swift Iris, to Poseidon the lord
all these things to announce, and not a false messenger to be.
sentences.i: “Be off with you, swift Iris, and announce all this to lord Poseidon, and do not be a false messenger.
sentences.n: βάσκ’ ἴθι is a double command, ‘go, set out’; βάσκε is an imperative of a verb for rapid going, and ἴθι the imperative of εἶμι. Ἶρι ταχεῖα is ‘swift Iris’ in the vocative. Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is ‘to Poseidon the lord’, the dative of the person told. Both infinitives, ἀγγεῖλαι ‘announce’ and εἶναι ‘be’, are commands. ψευδάγγελος is ψευδ- ‘false’ + ἄγγελος ‘messenger’; μὴ δέ is written apart, as ‘and not’.

sentences.t:
παυσάμενόν μιν ἄνωχθι μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο
ἔρχεσθαι μετὰ φῦλα θεῶν ἢ εἰς ἅλα δῖαν.
sentences.tr:
pausamenon min anōchthi machēs ēde ptolemoio
erchesthai meta phyla theōn ē eis hala dian.
sentences.l:
Having ceased from battle and from war, bid him
to go among the tribes of the gods or into the heavenly brine.
sentences.i: Bid him cease from battle and war, and go among the tribes of the gods or into the heavenly brine.
sentences.n: παυσάμενον is the aorist middle participle of παύω, ‘having stopped’, agreeing with μιν ‘him’, Poseidon; ἄνωχθι is the imperative of ἄνωγα ‘bid’. μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο is ‘from battle and war’. Poseidon is to go either μετὰ φῦλα θεῶν ‘among the tribes of the gods’ or to the sea, ἅλα δῖαν, ‘the heavenly brine’ (δῖα, the house word ‘heavenly’, even of the sea).

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μοι οὐκ ἐπέεσσ’ ἐπιπείσεται, ἀλλ’ ἀλογήσει,
φραζέσθω δὴ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
μή μ’ οὐδὲ κρατερός περ ἐὼν ἐπιόντα ταλάσσῃ
μεῖναι,
sentences.tr:
ei de moi ouk epeess’ epipeisetai, all’ alogēsei,
phrazesthō dē epeita kata phrena kai kata thymon
mē m’ oude krateros per eōn epionta talassēi
meinai,
sentences.l:
But if to my words he will not give heed, but will disregard them,
let him take heed then in his mind and in his heart
lest not even, strong though he is, as I come against him, he bring himself
to await me,
sentences.i: But if he does not obey my words and disregards them, let him then take care, in his mind and heart, lest, strong though he is, he fail even to bring himself to await me as I come against him,
sentences.n: The long sentence is cut here at the comma. ἐπιπείσεται ‘will obey’ (ἐπιπείθομαι) takes the dative ἐπέεσσ’; ἀλογήσει ‘will take no account’. φραζέσθω is the imperative ‘let him take heed’. μή … ταλάσσῃ is a clause of fear: ‘lest he not bring himself’, with ταλάσσῃ the aorist subjunctive of τλάω (‘bring oneself’ to do something hard), μεῖναι ‘to await’. ἐπιόντα ‘me as I come’ is the accusative participle, with κρατερός περ ἐών ‘strong though he is’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεί εὑ φημὶ βίῃ πολὺ φέρτερος εἶναι
καὶ γενεῇ πρότερος·
sentences.tr:
epei heu phēmi biēi poly pherteros einai
kai geneēi proteros·
sentences.l:
since I say that I myself am far stronger in might
and earlier in birth;
sentences.i: since I say that I am far stronger in might and older in birth;
sentences.n: εὑ is the old reflexive ‘myself’, here the subject of εἶναι. φέρτερος ‘stronger’ and πρότερος ‘earlier’ are comparatives; γενεῇ is the dative of respect, ‘in birth’, so ‘older’. Zeus rests his claim on strength and seniority.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ οὐκ ὄθεται φίλον ἦτορ
ἶσον ἐμοὶ φάσθαι, τόν τε στυγέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ ouk othetai philon ētor
ison emoi phasthai, ton te stygeousi kai alloi.
sentences.l:
of him the dear heart takes no heed
to say itself equal to me, whom others too hate.”
sentences.i: and his dear heart takes no heed to call himself my equal, though I am the one whom others too hate.”
sentences.n: τοῦ is Poseidon, owner of the ἦτορ ‘heart’; ὄθεται, ‘heeds, takes care’, takes the infinitive φάσθαι, ‘to say’: his heart takes no care about claiming equality. ἶσον ἐμοί is ‘equal to me’. τόν τε στυγέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι is ‘whom others too hate’, as it was said of Hector at 7.111; the antecedent is most naturally Zeus himself, the speaker, and the same words come at 183. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις,
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse podēnemos ōkea Iris,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, wind-footed, swift Iris,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Iris, wind-footed and swift, did not disobey;
sentences.n: This line is repeated whole from earlier in the poem. ἔφατ’ is ‘he spoke’, and ποδήνεμος ὠκέα Ἶρις is the pair of epithets ‘wind-footed, swift’. ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’, negated: she obeys.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρήν.
sentences.tr: bē de kat’ Idaiōn oreōn eis Ilion hirēn.
sentences.l: and she went down from the Idaean mountains to sacred Ilium.
sentences.i: and she went down from the Idaean mountains to sacred Ilium.
sentences.n: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘went’; κατ’ is ‘down’, with the genitive ὀρέων ‘from the mountains’. Ἰδαίων ὀρέων is ‘the Idaean mountains’, the range round Ida. ἱρήν is the Ionic ἱερήν ‘sacred’, an epithet of Ilium. Another whole line repeated from earlier.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἐκ νεφέων πτῆται νιφὰς ἠὲ χάλαζα
ψυχρὴ ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς αἰθρηγενέος Βορέαο,
ὣς κραιπνῶς μεμαυῖα διέπτατο ὠκέα Ἶρις,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an ek nepheōn ptētai niphas ēe chalaza
psychrē hypo rhipēs aithrēgeneos Boreao,
hōs kraipnōs memauia dieptato ōkea Iris,
sentences.l:
And as when from the clouds there flies snow or hail,
cold, under the blast of the North Wind, born of the clear sky,
so at a rush, eager, flew across swift Iris,
sentences.i: As snow or cold hail flies from the clouds under the blast of the North Wind, born of the clear sky, so, at a rush and in her eagerness, swift Iris flew across,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … πτῆται is a simile, ‘as when … flies’ (the subjunctive). νιφάς is ‘snow’, χάλαζα ‘hail’, and ψυχρή ‘cold’ goes with them. ῥιπῆς … Βορέαο is ‘the blast of the North Wind’, whose epithet αἰθρηγενής probably means ‘born of the clear sky’ (αἴθρη ‘clear sky’ + root of γίγνομαι); its exact sense is not certain. The comparison is completed by ὣς: κραιπνῶς is ‘at a rush’, μεμαυῖα the participle ‘eager’, and διέπτατο ‘flew across’; the half-line is the one said of Hera at 15.83.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη κλυτὸν ἐννοσίγαιον·
sentences.tr: anchou d’ histamenē prosephē klyton ennosigaion·
sentences.l: and standing close by, she addressed the famous earth-shaker:
sentences.i: She came and stood close by, and said to the famous earth-shaker:
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη is the standard way to bring a messenger or god to a person’s side; the subject, Iris, is carried over from the simile. κλυτὸν ἐννοσίγαιον is ‘the famous earth-shaker’, Poseidon, the stock epithet κλυτός ‘famous’ with ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἀγγελίην τινά τοι γαιήοχε κυανοχαῖτα
ἦλθον δεῦρο φέρουσα παραὶ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.tr:
angeliēn tina toi gaiēoche kyanochaita
ēlthon deuro pherousa parai Dios aigiochoio.
sentences.l:
“News, a certain piece, for you, earth-holder, dark-haired one,
I have come here bringing, from beside aegis-bearing Zeus.
sentences.i: “Earth-holder, dark-haired one, I have come here from aegis-bearing Zeus, bringing you some news.
sentences.n: ἀγγελίην is ‘news’, with τινά ‘some’; τοι is ‘for you’. γαιήοχε κυανοχαῖτα are the vocative epithets of Poseidon, ‘earth-holder, dark-haired one’, stock epithets, γαιήοχος ‘earth-holder’ (the usual explanation of the second half) and κυανοχαίτης ‘dark-haired’. ἦλθον is ‘I have come’, φέρουσα ‘bringing’, and παραὶ is παρά, ‘from beside’. Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο is ‘aegis-bearing Zeus’, the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
παυσάμενόν σ’ ἐκέλευσε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο
ἔρχεσθαι μετὰ φῦλα θεῶν ἢ εἰς ἅλα δῖαν.
sentences.tr:
pausamenon s’ ekeleuse machēs ēde ptolemoio
erchesthai meta phyla theōn ē eis hala dian.
sentences.l:
Having ceased from battle and from war, he bade you
to go among the tribes of the gods or into the heavenly brine.
sentences.i: He has bidden you cease from battle and war, and go among the tribes of the gods or into the heavenly brine.
sentences.n: Iris repeats Zeus’s own order (160–161) almost exactly, changing only the pronouns: παυσάμενον … σ’ ἐκέλευσε is ‘he bade you, having ceased’. The English is the same as there.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ οἱ οὐκ ἐπέεσσ’ ἐπιπείσεαι, ἀλλ’ ἀλογήσεις,
ἠπείλει καὶ κεῖνος ἐναντίβιον πολεμίξων
ἐνθάδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
ei de hoi ouk epeess’ epipeiseai, all’ alogēseis,
ēpeilei kai keinos enantibion polemixōn
enthad’ eleusesthai·
sentences.i: But if you do not obey his words and disregard them, he threatened that he too would come here to fight you head-on;
sentences.n: Iris continues, repeating 162 in the second person: ἐπιπείσεαι and ἀλογήσεις are the future ‘you will obey’, ‘you will take no account’. ἠπείλει is the imperfect of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, with the infinitive ἐλεύσεσθαι ‘would come’; καὶ κεῖνος is ‘he too’. ἐναντίβιον πολεμίξων is ‘head-on to fight’, the participle of purpose.

sentences.t:
σὲ δ’ ὑπεξαλέασθαι ἄνωγε
χεῖρας, ἐπεὶ σέο φησὶ βίῃ πολὺ φέρτερος εἶναι
καὶ γενεῇ πρότερος·
sentences.tr:
se d’ hypexaleasthai anōge
cheiras, epei seo phēsi biēi poly pherteros einai
kai geneēi proteros·
sentences.i: and he bids you slip away from his hands, since he says he is far stronger than you in might and older in birth;
sentences.n: ὑπεξαλέασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of a verb ‘slip away from under, avoid’; χεῖρας is its object, ‘his hands’, i.e. Zeus’s grasp. σέο is σοῦ (genitive of comparison) after φέρτερος ‘stronger’, and the rest repeats 165–166, which Zeus said of himself.

sentences.t:
σὸν δ’ οὐκ ὄθεται φίλον ἦτορ
ἶσόν οἱ φάσθαι, τόν τε στυγέουσι καὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr:
son d’ ouk othetai philon ētor
ison hoi phasthai, ton te stygeousi kai alloi.
sentences.l:
your dear heart takes no heed
to say itself equal to him, whom others too hate.”
sentences.i: and your dear heart takes no heed to call yourself his equal, though he is the one whom others too hate.”
sentences.n: This is 166–167 again with the pronouns turned round: σόν ‘your’ for τοῦ, and οἱ ‘to him’ for ἐμοί, so that τόν, ‘whom’, most naturally means Zeus (as in the earlier line). ὄθεται and φάσθαι are as before. Iris’s speech, and the part, end here; Poseidon’s reply opens the next.
